state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Great job on identifying that it is a translation by a vector! Let's focus on the specific translation involved when we have \( f(x-3) \). turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so I think I get that \( f(x-3) \) actually moves the graph to the right instead of up. So maybe the translation vector should be \(\left[\begin{array}{l} 3 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]\)? But I'm still a bit confused about why it moves to the right instead of up. Can you explain that part again?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track with recognizing that \( f(x-3) \) moves the graph to the right. Think about how the function \( f(x - a) \) affects the x-values of the graph. Consider how changing the input variable x by a affects the output of the function. Can you apply this idea to determine the correct translation vector for this specific case?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I see it a bit better now! So when we have \( f(x-3) \), it means we're actually replacing x with a smaller number, which makes the graph move to the right by 3 units. But I'm still a bit confused about why it works that way. Can you help me understand why changing x like that makes it shift right instead of up?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher never directly addresses why the student initially thought the transformation was vertical (the core misconception), instead offering generic prompts that lead the student to the correct answer without understanding why their original reasoning was wrong, as evidenced by the student's persistent confusion in Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently scaffolds by breaking down the transformation concept, provides appropriate prompts that guide without telling, and adjusts support based on student progress from initial misconception to near-correct understanding, though could have provided slightly more concrete scaffolding when the student remained confused in Turn 4.
